rationale: A wins because it stays close to the announcement and turns the missing pieces into proof demands instead of pretending they are proof. A's "An unprofitable automaker turns its charging network into a revenue line" gives a markets reporter a real, testable tension; B's "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" invents a fight the update does not support. B has usable bones, but too much of it is trend garnish wearing a reporter badge.
gaps_in_A: "Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs — the connector fight is over" overclaims. One company's dual-connector plan does not prove the connector fight is over.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks" imports outside market context without evidence from the update. Fine as a reporting question, not as a settled premise.
"competing for the same drivers rather than negotiating with their manufacturers" leans too hard on "no partnership announced." No announced partnership is not proof of a go-it-alone strategy.
gaps_in_B: "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" is the bad kind of spicy. The facts mention Tesla-style NACS plugs, not a Tesla competitive campaign.
"following the industry's shift away from automaker-exclusive plugs" is a broad trend claim the update does not prove. It needs outside sourcing before it belongs in the angle.
"charging networks that were once brand perks are becoming shared utilities" dresses a single company announcement as an industry thesis. That is not grounding; that is wallpaper.
"without a single automaker partner to show for it" turns absence into attitude. The supplied fact is only that no partnership was announced.
